definition: A standard text format (JWT) for a set of signed claims; Harbor Cards are written in it, and the format itself grants no authority.
The rule that the verifier, never the card, chooses how a signature is checked: the allowed algorithm and key type come from the verifier's own trusted policy.
Withdrawing a card before it expires, so that a verifier that has received the withdrawal refuses the card.

As a verb: a daemon periodically sends what it knows to a few other daemons, which pass it on in turn, until every daemon has it. As an adjective (gossip protocol, gossip mesh): a set of daemons that spreads information this way, or the rules they follow to do it.
One delegation step, from a parent card's holder to a child card's holder.
A tag computed with a secret key (HMAC is one kind), where the same key both creates and checks the tag, so anyone who can check a tag can also make one.
An attack on a verifier that believes the algorithm named in a token's header: the attacker names no algorithm, or names one under which a published public key works as a secret key.
A fresh random value included in a signature to tie it to one particular exchange; on its own it does not stop a copied message from being replayed.
A tool that checks a protocol's messages against an attacker who controls the network, treating the cryptography as perfect, over any number of protocol runs.

A compact, approximate set that stores a short fingerprint of each key in one of two buckets and supports deletion; it can wrongly report a key as present but, used correctly, never wrongly reports a stored key as absent.
A filter's report that an item is present when it is not, such as a card reported as revoked that was never revoked.
A list of counters, one per daemon, recording how many of each daemon's updates a copy of a shared log has seen, so that copies can be compared and merged in order.
An older compact, approximate set that sets a few bits per key and cannot delete a key, so whole filters must be replaced on a schedule.
The maximum fraction of a filter's slots allowed to be full (95 percent in Port Daddy's cuckoo-filter library); above it insertions start to fail and the false-positive bound no longer holds.
A form of gossip in which each round a daemon compares its copy of the data with a randomly chosen peer's and each copies what the other lacks.
An attacker who can read, alter and inject any network message but cannot break the cryptography; the standard attacker of symbolic protocol analysis.
A verification tool for Rust code that checks a function on every input within stated limits and reports any input that breaks an assertion.
Checking code on every input within stated size limits instead of on a few test inputs; a result says nothing about inputs beyond the limits.
A request to the checker to find at least one input that reaches a stated outcome, which shows that passing assertions are not passing merely because no input reaches the code.
A deliberate breakage of the code that a working check must catch, used to show the check can fail.

A rule for presenting a card: whoever shows it must also sign the request with the private key the card names, so that copied card bytes alone authorize nothing. The daemon does not implement it. Chapter 2 builds it for this book's kernel.

A signature that tells a gate to take one card back. It is made over the harbor's key and the card's id, by the harbor or by a holder the card's chain names. It answers no challenge, so every gate can check the same one.
